title: DEEP BATCH ACTIVE LEARNING BY DIVERSE, UNCERTAIN GRADIENT LOWER BOUNDS

elements.name: Pool-based batch active learning setting
elements.description: An unlabeled pool supplies examples, the learner queries labels for selected batches, and a neural classifier is trained using as few queries as possible.
elements.source_text: We consider the pool-based active learning setup, where the learner receives an unlabeled dataset U sampled according to  $D_{\mathcal X}$  and can request labels sampled according to  $D_{\mathcal Y|\mathcal X}$  for any  $x\in U$ .

elements.name: Neural classifier and cross-entropy training objective
elements.description: The classifier predicts the highest-scoring class and network parameters are trained by minimizing cross-entropy on the labeled set.
elements.source_text: We optimize the parameters by minimizing the cross-entropy loss  $\mathbb{E}_S[\ell_{\mathrm{CE}}(f(x; \theta), y)]$  over the labeled examples, where  $\ell_{\mathrm{CE}}(p, y) = \sum_{i=1}^K I(y=i) \ln 1/p_i = \ln 1/p_y$ .
elements.pseudocode: loss = mean(cross_entropy(model(x), y) for x, y in labeled_set); update model parameters to minimize loss

elements.name: BADGE batch active learning
elements.description: BADGE initializes a labeled set, repeatedly computes hallucinated last-layer gradient embeddings for the remaining pool, samples a diverse batch with k-MEANS++, queries labels, retrains from the accumulated labeled data, and returns the final model.
elements.source_text:
1: Labeled dataset  $S \leftarrow M$  examples drawn uniformly at random from U together with queried labels.
2: Train an initial model  $\theta_1$  on S by minimizing  $\mathbb{E}_S[\ell_{CE}(f(x;\theta),y)]$ .
3: **for**  $t = 1, 2, \dots, T$ : **do**
4: For all examples x in  $U \setminus S$ :
  - 1: Compute its hypothetical label  $\hat{y}(x) = h_{\theta_t}(x)$ .
  - 2: Compute gradient embedding  $g_x = \frac{\partial}{\partial \theta_{\text{out}}} \ell_{\text{CE}}(f(x;\theta), \hat{y}(x))|_{\theta=\theta_t}$ , where  $\theta_{\text{out}}$  refers to parameters of the final (output) layer.
5: Compute  $S_t$ , a random subset of  $U \setminus S$ , using the k-MEANS++ seeding algorithm on  $\{g_x : x \in U \setminus S\}$  and query for their labels.
6:  $S \leftarrow S \cup S_t$ .
7: Train a model  $\theta_{t+1}$  on S by minimizing  $\mathbb{E}_S[\ell_{CE}(f(x;\theta),y)]$ .
8: end for
9: **return** Final model  $\theta_{T+1}$ .
elements.pseudocode: S = uniform_sample(U, M); query labels(S); theta = train_cross_entropy(S); for t in 1..T: candidates = U - S; for x in candidates: y_hat[x] = argmax(model(theta, x)); g[x] = gradient_last_layer(cross_entropy(model(theta, x), y_hat[x])); S_t = kmeans_plus_plus(g, B); query labels(S_t); S = S union S_t; theta = train_cross_entropy(S); return theta

elements.name: Hallucinated label
elements.description: The current model prediction is used as a proxy label so a gradient can be computed before the true label is queried.
elements.source_text: for every x in the pool U, we compute the label  $\hat{y}(x)$  preferred by the current model

elements.name: Hallucinated final-layer gradient embedding
elements.description: The gradient of cross-entropy under the predicted label is used as the embedding for acquisition; in softmax networks each output-layer block is a probability residual times the penultimate representation.
elements.pseudocode: for class i: g_block[i] = (p[i] - indicator(y_hat == i)) * penultimate_features

elements.name: Softmax cross-entropy in last-layer parameterization
elements.description: For a softmax output over a penultimate representation, cross-entropy is expressed in terms of output-layer weights and logits.
elements.pseudocode: loss = log(sum(exp(W[j] dot z) for j in classes)) - W[y] dot z

elements.name: k-MEANS++ seeding sampler
elements.description: Sequentially selects the first embedding uniformly and each later embedding with probability proportional to squared distance from its nearest selected center.
elements.source_text:
C_1 \leftarrow \{c_1\}, where c_1 is sampled uniformly at random from G.

for t = 2, \ldots, k: do

Define D_t(x) := \min_{c \in C_{t-1}} \|x - c\|_2.

c_t \leftarrow \text{Sample } x \text{ from } G \text{ with probability } \frac{D_t(x)^2}{\sum_{x \in G} D_t(x)^2}.
elements.pseudocode: C = {uniform_sample(G)}; while len(C) < k: distance[x] = min squared distance from x to C; choose x with probability distance[x] / sum(distance); C.add(x); return C

elements.name: Predicted-label gradient is a lower bound
elements.description: Under the stated neural-network structure, the norm of the hallucinated final-layer gradient is no larger than the norm induced by any true label, so it conservatively measures potential model influence.
elements.source_text: We show in Proposition I that, assuming a common structure satisfied by most natural neural networks, the gradient norm with respect to the last layer using this label provides a lower bound on the gradient norm induced by any other label.

elements.name: True-label gradient norm
elements.description: The squared norm of a true-label last-layer gradient factors into a probability-dependent term and the squared norm of the penultimate representation.
elements.pseudocode: gradient_norm_squared = (sum(p[i]^2 for i in classes) + 1 - 2 * p[y]) * squared_norm(z)

elements.name: Embedding magnitude captures predictive uncertainty
elements.description: Confident predictions produce small hallucinated gradient embeddings, while uncertain predictions produce larger embeddings and are more likely to be selected.
elements.source_text: if the model is highly certain about the example's label, then the example's gradient embedding will have a small norm, and vice versa for samples where the model is uncertain

elements.name: Joint diversity and uncertainty selection
elements.description: k-MEANS++ favors large and distant gradient embeddings, combining uncertainty through magnitude with batch diversity through directions without a hand-tuned tradeoff hyperparameter.
elements.source_text: k-MEANS++ seeding selects centroids by iteratively sampling points in proportion to their squared distances from the nearest centroid that has already been chosen, which, like a k-DPP, tends to select a diverse batch of high-magnitude samples.
elements.pseudocode: selection_weight[x] = squared_distance_to_nearest_selected_embedding(x); sample next point proportional to selection_weight

elements.name: BADGE robustness across datasets, architectures, and batch sizes
elements.description: Evaluate BADGE in repeated pool-based active-learning runs across image and OpenML datasets, MLP, ResNet, and VGG architectures, and batch sizes 100, 1000, and 10000.
elements.source_text: We consider three neural network architectures: a two-layer Perceptron with ReLU activations (MLP), an 18-layer convolutional ResNet ..., and an 11-layer VGG network ... We evaluate our algorithms using three image datasets, SVHN, CIFAR10 and MNIST ... and four non-image datasets from the OpenML repository (#6, #155, #156, and #184).
elements.pseudocode: for dataset, architecture, batch_size in experiment_settings: run BADGE active learning; record test accuracy versus queried labels

elements.name: Initial set, rounds, and batch size
elements.description: BADGE uses M initial randomly labeled examples, T acquisition rounds, and batch size B; the experiments fix M at 100 and vary B over 100, 1000, and 10000.
elements.source_text: To ensure a comprehensive comparison among all algorithms, we evaluate them in a batch-mode active learning setup with M=100 being the number of initial random labeled examples and batch size B varying from  $\{100,1000,10000\}$ .
elements.pseudocode: M = 100; B in {100, 1000, 10000}; choose T according to pool and budget

elements.name: Training protocol
elements.description: Retrain from scratch after each acquisition round with Adam until training accuracy exceeds 99%, using fixed learning rates and no schedules or augmentation.
elements.source_text: We fit models using cross-entropy loss and the Adam variant of SGD until training accuracy exceeds 99%. We use a learning rate of 0.001 for image data and of 0.0001 for non-image data. We avoid warm starting and retrain models from scratch every time new samples are queried. All experiments are repeated five times. No learning rate schedules or data augmentation are used.
elements.pseudocode: for each round: initialize model from scratch; optimize cross_entropy with Adam until training_accuracy > 0.99; repeat five seeds
